concept.name: Market profile
concept.definition: A charting method developed by J. Peter Steidlmayer at the Chicago Board of Trade in the 1980s that organizes a session's trading as a distribution: each price traded during each time bracket (conventionally 30 minutes, labeled A, B, C…) receives that bracket's letter, building a horizontal histogram of time-at-price. It is a way of organizing market-generated data for auction-market analysis — a chart format, not an indicator or a predictive system.
concept.intuition: Instead of plotting price against time, the profile plots time spent at each price, revealing where the market accepted value (fat middle) and where it rejected prices (thin tails).
concept.mechanics: The session is divided into brackets; every price traded in a bracket gets that bracket's TPO letter; the stacked letters form the distribution from which the point of control (longest row), value area (~70% of TPOs), initial balance, single prints, and tails are read.
concept.failure_modes: Profile reading depends on subjective session definitions and bracket conventions, and its day-type labels are assigned in hindsight; applying its shape heuristics mechanically, without the underlying auction logic, degrades into curve-fit pattern matching.
concept.misconceptions: Market Profile is not a trading system with built-in signals — its own documentation stresses it is a way of organizing market-generated data; nor is it the same as a volume profile, which counts contracts rather than time brackets.
concept.example: A day's ES session prints brackets A through J; the D–G rows stack widest around 4,520 (the POC) and 70% of TPOs sit between 4,512 and 4,531 (the value area), with single B-period prints at the low marking an early rejection.
